g.passage: Brakes shrieked somewhere under the floor, and the compartment smelled of wet wool and the oranges my father had been peeling since we left Krakow. He had my article open on his knee again. For the third time that morning he was translating it, line by line, for Tatiana, a woman with a cello case who had made the mistake of asking where we were going. His Polish turned my four modest paragraphs into something closer to a speech. I told him the piece was about drainage policy and that no one on earth needed to hear it twice. He nodded and kept going. I was not embarrassed, exactly; I had simply heard the paragraph about storm grates often enough to recite it. At Tarnów, Tatiana got off, and my father folded the page into careful quarters. When he dozed against the window, I took the spare copy from my own bag, smoothed its creases, and tucked it into the pocket of his coat, beneath his ticket.

Ximena waited with a sack of seedlings she had bought before she had anywhere to put them. A man in a straw hat, Emiliano, waited too. While they stood there he pointed out which beds belonged to whom, which faucet leaked, and which neighbor would lend a hoe if asked twice. He told her that the first month was the hardest and that the soil here forgave mistakes. On the fence beside them hung a tin sign with a plot number painted over in blue. Neither of them mentioned it. When the coordinator finally arrived, out of breath, she unlocked the gate and handed out two sets of keys. She asked Emiliano to sign the register under the heading for new members, just below the line where Ximena had written her name. He took off his hat to do it, then stood holding the pen a moment longer than the signature required.

A sari, he said, had to be halved, then halved again, the border kept outward so a customer could see the work at once. He made me do it forty times one afternoon, until the creases lay flat as pressed leaves. 'One day these shelves are yours,' he said, and went back to his ledger. On the top shelf, behind the starch tins, sat a letter with a Poona postmark that nobody opened while I was in the room. Two years later I told him about the teaching post in Poona. He did not answer. That evening I found my trunk on the counter, already filled, every blouse and sari halved and halved again, borders turned outward, and the lid left open for me to close.

g.passage: Three rules governed Miss Kai's shop on Harbour Street: measure twice, cut once, and walk the sea wall every Sunday after chapel. The first two I understood. The third she never explained. Each week in that summer of 1861 we went along the promenade at Kingston, she with her parasol, I a step behind with my hands still smelling of chalk, and each week she stopped at the same iron bench to watch the fishing boats come in. 'When you keep a shop of your own,' she said once, 'you will know why.' In her workroom lay a bolt of blue linen that she dusted but did not cut. Thirty years on, my own shop has a sign over the door and a boy who threads needles faster than I ever did. On Sundays he walks a step behind me. I stop at the iron bench. He has not yet asked why, and I have not yet decided what I would tell him.

It shows how a mentor's unexplained Sunday habit has passed into the narrator's own life.

It suggests that the narrator's apprentice led him to recall his mentor's weekly walk.

g.passage: We arrived at the Posillipo pool at seven, because Elisa said the salt water was flattest before the swim club came. My brother brought goggles. She confiscated them. Her method had four parts, which she listed like train stops: lie back, ears under, hands open, stop trying. Fishermen's sons had learned it on this coast before anyone sold inflatable rings, she said, and now the sons sold inflatable rings. My brother sank eleven times. 'Count, Giada,' Elisa told me, so I counted from the bench, where the tiles were warm and someone had left half a lemon ice. On the twelfth try he drifted for perhaps nine seconds, arms out, staring at the sky. Elisa did not clap. g.passage: Glue and tar and old paper: that is what the workshop on Jalan Kembang Jepun smells like, and the tar comes from your rope. You carried it off Matteo's freighter four years ago, coiled around a bundle of clothes, when the captain found you behind the rice sacks and, instead of calling the harbor police, brought you here. In the workshop the rope is useful. You tie finished stacks of ledgers with it for delivery, then untie it and coil it again by your bench, always beside the cloth bundle you never quite unpack. Matteo, who binds books now instead of sailing, has stopped asking about the bundle. This year he taught you headbands, the small stitched cords at the top of a spine. On Friday you take the rope, unpick it strand by strand, and sew the strands into the headband of a ledger for the harbor office. Then you shake the bundle open, Putri, and fold your shirts into the drawer under the bench.

g.passage: I worked the customs booth at the Haifa road checkpoint that spring, and I watched the red stakes come. Amit, the surveyor from the city, drove them himself, one every twenty meters, along the line on his blueprint, which crossed Avraham's orchard behind my booth. Avraham drove his crates past me each morning and did not look at them. In May a wind came off the bay and bent his youngest fig nearly to the ground. When I passed at noon, one of the red stakes had been pulled from the line and driven in beside the fig, the trunk bound to it with a strip of sacking. Amit saw it on his rounds. He stood a long time with his blueprint. Then he took a fresh stake from his truck, measured a meter past the fig's roots, hammered it in there, and erased something on the paper with the end of his pencil.

g.passage: Nadeesha, Father Xiulan said, as if he had seen me the Sunday before rather than three years ago, and he pressed a hymnal into my hands because the hall at the Railway Hotel had more guests than chairs. We talked about the bride's lace, the rain, the price of a ticket to Dublin. We did not talk about the choir loft at St. Nicholas, where I had stood every Sunday until my brother's funeral.
